newsitem.title: USA: Iraq no-fire policy holding in no-fly zones - U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iraq no-fire policy holding in no-fly zones - U.S..

text.p: The United States sees no sign that Iraq has changed its policy of not firing at Western allied planes patrolling the no-fly zones over the country, a White House spokesman said on Sunday.

"There is not an indication at this point of any change in the position ... of the overall disposition toward the no-fly zone," spokesman Michael McCurry told reporters accompanying President Bill Clinton on a campaign trip in Florida.
He spoke after Iraq denied a White House statement that a U.S. F-16 jet had fired a missile at a radar installation in southern Iraq on Saturday.
The Iraqi News Agency quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesman dismissing the White House statement as "false news" aimed at helping Clinton win re-election.
"Such American allegations are baseless. No incident of any kind has occurred in Iraq's airspace," the spokesman was quoted as saying.
"Fabricating this false news is part of the U.S. election campaign, the U.S. style," INA quoted him as saying.
The spokesman said Iraq was still committed to a decision not to fire at U.S. and allied jets patrolling the two no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq.
The decision was taken in September after a confrontation with the United States because of Baghdad's backing of a Kurdish group against a rival in the north.
The United States responded by attacking southern Iraq with missiles and extending the southern no-fly zone for Iraqi planes to the outskirts of Baghdad.

The White House confirmed late on Saturday a Washington Times report on the missile incident. It said a U.S. Air Force F-16 jet enforcing the no-fly zone in southern Iraq had been targeted by Iraqi radar and had fired on the Iraqi installation in response.
The plane returned to base without incident. Clinton was informed of the incident, which took place about 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT) on Saturday, White House spokesman Barry Toiv said.
The spokesman said the pilot of the F-16 believed he had been targeted by missile-tracking radar, a hostile act that allows U.S. pilots to fire missiles in retaliation.
The F-16 pilot fired a single High-Speed Anti-Radiation Missile (HARM) at what he believed was a mobile surface-to-air missile battery.
